title: The Fire and the Lions
lead: God does not always remove the fire, but He is in it with us. Faithfulness makes sense even when it seems to lead to disaster.
questions: Which orchestra is playing loudest around you, and is your daily kneeling preparing you for the day it plays with the full ensemble?
Does your faith already contain the words “But if not,” or are you still setting conditions for God?
What fire in your life did not go out, but burned away your bonds, and can you recognize the presence of the Fourth in it?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: Babylon began by changing names: four Hebrew confessions of faith were replaced with Babylonian ones. But you can wear someone else’s name on the payroll and your own in your heart. On the plain of Dura, Nebuchadnezzar set up a statue made entirely of gold, correcting the prophecy in which only the head was made of the noblest metal, and he staged a spectacle of conformity with an orchestra: the music plays, everyone falls down. Against the backdrop of thousands of bowed backs stand three figures. These men’s answer is one of the most mature confessions of faith in Scripture: our God is able to deliver us, “But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods” (WEB). Faith that says “but if not” no longer sets conditions for the Creator.

God did not put out the furnace or take them out of the fire. He went into it with them: the king saw four men, “unbound and unharmed, walking around in the fire,” and “the fourth looks like a son of the gods!” They fell in bound and walked around free; the only thing the fire burned was their bonds. Decades later, Daniel, now in his eighties, an official without a single blemish, fell into a trap made out of his own faithfulness: a decree forbidding prayer. When he learned of it, he went home, to the room whose windows opened toward Jerusalem, and prayed three times a day, “just as he had done before.” He staged no protest and hid nothing: he simply changed nothing. People survive their lions’ dens thanks to habits of kneeling built long before the decree.

What happens next? A stone rolled over the mouth of the den, the royal seal, a sleepless night, dawn, a question asked at the tomb, and a man alive inside: “My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions.” All the props of a certain morning outside Jerusalem, only six hundred years earlier. The stories of the three young men and of Daniel end the same way: a pagan ruler writes a hymn to the living God addressed to all nations. It was earned by four exiles who did nothing but one thing: they did not stop being themselves.

Today we begin the section “There Is Hope When You Are Far from Home.” This week’s heroes are exiles: people torn from their homeland, living in a culture that does not understand them and sometimes openly wants to remake them in its own image. Today’s two stories are about people at different stages of life. Into the furnace go young men just starting out; into the lions’ den goes a gray-haired official past eighty. Pressure does not ask your age. Neither does faithfulness.

sections.heading: Four Names
paragraphs: Babylon began its work on the boys carried off from Judah with something seemingly harmless: changing their names, which in that world amounted to a confession of faith. The names of the Hebrew young men clearly point to the God of Israel. The meaning of some of the Babylonian names they were given is uncertain and is reconstructed in different ways. But we do know that the new names tied them to the culture and religion of Babylon. That is what they were called from then on, every day: in the corridors, in the documents, at the table. The empire knew what it was doing: whoever changes your name is trying to control your identity. And yet the whole book of Daniel is proof that you can wear someone else’s name on the payroll and your own in your heart. The world may call you by its own names. That does not have to change who you are inside.

sections.heading: A Statue All of Gold
paragraphs: The chapter before describes Nebuchadnezzar’s dream of a statue made of four metals: only the head was gold, and it stood for him, and after him other kingdoms were to come. On the plain of Dura the king sets up a corrected statue: sixty cubits high, all gold, from head to toe. He did not reject the prophecy. He edited it: he extended himself over the whole future. Then he summons the entire administration of the empire and stages a spectacle of conformity with full production values: a herald, the threat of the furnace, and an orchestra. The narrator deliberately repeats the list of instruments, again and again, “the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipes, and all kinds of music,” until it starts to sound like a parody of this liturgy of coercion. The music plays, everyone falls down. From a bird’s-eye view the plain of Dura looks perfect: thousands of backs bowing in the same rhythm. And it is precisely against this choreography that we see three figures still standing.

sections.heading: But If Not
paragraphs: An accusation comes at once, and the king flies into a rage, but he gives them a second chance: the music will play, bow down, for “what god will be able to deliver you from my hands?” The answer of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego is one of the most mature confessions of faith in all of Scripture: “our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace; and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods, nor worship the golden image which you have set up” (WEB). We need to hear both halves of this statement. The first is full of trust: our God is able. The second breathes something rarer than trust: “But if not.” They have no guarantee of rescue, and they do not pretend to have one. Their faithfulness is not a transaction in which God pays for obedience with deliverance. Faith with a “but if not” clause is trust that has stopped setting conditions for the Creator. This kind is fireproof even before the furnace.

sections.heading: The Fourth in the Fire
paragraphs: The furnace was heated seven times hotter than usual, so hot that the flames killed the executioners themselves. Three bound men fell inside. And then the king jumped up in alarm: “Did we not throw three men, firmly bound, into the fire?… I see four men, unbound and unharmed, walking around in the fire,” and “the fourth looks like a son of the gods!” The heart of today’s scene lies in these words. God did not put out the furnace, nor did He keep His people from going into the fire. But the king saw a fourth figure among them, and later he himself said that God had sent His angel. Isaiah recorded a promise given to the exiles: “When you walk through the fire, you will not be scorched; the flames will not set you ablaze.” Notice what this promise does not say: it does not say there will be no fire. It assumes there will be, and promises help inside it. On the plain of Dura, God kept it to the letter. One more detail is worth noticing: they fell in bound, and they walk around unbound. The only thing the fire burned was their bonds. There are fires in life from which a person comes out freer than they went in. At the king’s command they came out without a trace: “Not a hair of their heads was singed, their robes were unaffected, and there was no smell of fire on them.” And Nebuchadnezzar, the same man who an hour earlier had asked what god could deliver from his hands, now blesses this God, who “has sent His angel and delivered His servants.” Three mid-level officials, simply by not kneeling, did more for the witness to the Creator in Babylon than many a sermon. Sometimes the loudest confession of faith is standing up straight in silence.

sections.heading: A Window Open Toward Jerusalem
paragraphs: The second story takes place several decades and one empire later. Babylon has fallen, Darius rules, and Daniel, now a man past eighty, is one of the three highest officials in the state and is about to become the first of them. His rivals look for something to hang on him, and the text gives him the kind of testimonial every person in power could only dream of: “they could find no charge or corruption, because he was trustworthy, and no negligence or corruption was found in him.” Only one option is left to them: “unless we find something against him concerning the law of his God.” The only way to get this man is to turn his faithfulness into a crime. Flattering the king’s vanity, they push through a decree: for thirty days, no prayers to anyone but the king, on pain of the lions. And Daniel? “Now when Daniel learned that the document had been signed, he went into his house, where the windows of his upper room opened toward Jerusalem, and three times a day he got down on his knees, prayed, and gave thanks to his God, just as he had done before.” Just as he had done before. He staged no protest and hid nothing. He simply changed nothing. His strength was not the heroism of the moment, but a faithful routine: three times a day, his whole adult life, at a window open toward the home he had not seen since his youth. That window was not sentimentality. When Solomon dedicated the temple, he prayed for people who would one day be carried off to the land of their enemies: if there they return with all their heart “and when they pray to You in the direction of the land that You gave to their fathers,” hear them from heaven. Daniel knelt at that window like a man holding God to a word given four centuries earlier. Prayer in exile has, in the Bible, a promise older than the exile itself. People survive their lions’ dens thanks to a habit of prayer they built long before the decree.

sections.heading: The Stone and the Seal
paragraphs: The king, trapped by his own law, searches until sundown for a way to rescue Daniel and loses to his own signature. They throw Daniel into the den, roll a stone over its mouth, and the king seals it with his own signet ring and with the rings of his nobles, “so that nothing concerning Daniel could be changed.” Then he spends a night without sleep or entertainment, and at dawn he hurries to the den and cries out “in a voice of anguish”: “O Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the lions?” From the darkness comes the calm voice of an old man: “My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions.” Let us read the elements of this scene once more, slowly: an innocent man condemned, a pit closed with a stone, the seal of power on the stone, a sleepless night, dawn, a question asked at the tomb, and a living man whom death could not harm. All the props of a certain morning outside Jerusalem lie here together, six hundred years earlier. The text spells nothing out. Neither do we need to.

The story ends like the one about the furnace: a pagan ruler writes “to the people of every nation and language” a hymn about someone else’s God. “For He is the living God, and He endures forever… He delivers and rescues.” Two rulers of empires, Nebuchadnezzar and Darius, gave the God of Israel testimonials that no prophet could have written better. They were earned not by diplomats and armies, but by four exiles who, at the decisive moment, did nothing but one thing: they did not stop being themselves. Far from home, the greatest mission is sometimes simply faithfulness, because it is watched by people who look more closely than we think.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: The story from the plain of Dura has a sequel in the Bible: Revelation describes humanity’s final test with images taken straight from the third chapter of Daniel, including a statue, forced worship, and the threat of death. So this story is not a museum piece, but the pattern of a test that returns, on different scales, in every generation. Today it rarely looks like a furnace. More often it looks like an orchestra: everyone around you kneels to the same rhythm, and standing up straight costs you your position, your reputation, your peace and quiet. Let us draw three lessons from today’s stories. First: faith grows into the words “but if not.” God is worth our faithfulness even when He has not promised us a happy ending in this chapter. Second: God more often walks into the furnace than puts it out. In the Bible, the presence of the Fourth in the fire is a more frequent miracle than the absence of fire, and sometimes the flame burns away nothing but a person’s bonds. Third: the outcome of the day of testing is decided by the routine of ordinary days. Daniel survived the den because he had thousands of quiet kneelings at the window behind him. Take care of your window toward Jerusalem before anyone signs a decree.
